scenario: You've been working a bow drill for 25 minutes. Your willow spindle and willow fireboard came from branches lying on the ground after two days of rain. You get some smoke from the notch but the dust never holds as a coal. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Not enough downward pressure on the handhold
The wood is too damp - ground-lying wood after days of rain holds moisture
Willow is the wrong species for a bow drill
The bow is too long for the spindle

explanation: Damp wood is the most common reason a bow drill fails in the field. Moisture in the spindle and board soaks up the heat, so the dust never gets hot enough to form a coal. Wood lying on wet ground is the worst choice; dead wood still standing or hanging off the ground is drier, and splitting it exposes the drier core. Willow is a good bow drill wood, so species is not the problem. Pressure and notch shape matter, but even perfect technique will not overcome wet wood. Keeping the pieces inside your jacket for a while helps dry the surface.

scenario: Fires are allowed where you are camped. You have dry tinder (cattail fluff), sorted kindling, wrist-size dead wood, and a full bucket of water. Put these steps in the right order for a safe, reliable fire.

items.text: Clear a circle at least 10 feet across down to bare soil, away from tents, brush, and low branches
Place the tinder bundle in the center of the fire ring
Build a small teepee of the thinnest kindling over the tinder, leaving a door on the upwind side
Light the tinder at its base through the upwind door
Add thicker kindling, then wrist-size wood, one size at a time as each catches

explanation: Clear the site first - the Forest Service recommends a cleared circle about 10 feet across and keeping fires at least 15 feet from tents and vegetation, because stray embers landing in dry debris start many wildfires. Build from smallest to largest: tinder, then fine kindling. Light at the base on the upwind side so the breeze pushes flame into the fuel. Only after the fine kindling is burning do you add bigger pieces. Adding large wood too early smothers the fire and is the most common beginner mistake. Never leave the fire unattended.

start.scenario: It has rained for 3 days. Everything looks wet. You need fire to boil water for your group. You have 2 matches, a ferrocerium rod, and a fixed-blade knife, but no kit tinder. What's your first move?

options.text: Find standing dead wood and split it to reach the dry core
Look for natural tinder that resists water, like fatwood or birch bark

dead_standing.scenario: Good. Standing dead wood stays drier inside than wood on the ground. You find a dead branch about 4 inches thick still attached to a tree and break off a section. Now what?

options.text: Split it with your knife to expose the dry inner wood, then carve thin feather sticks
Break the dry inner wood into chunks and try to light the chunks directly

feather_sticks.explanation: Splitting dead wood to reach the dry core and carving fine feather sticks is the right wet-weather sequence. Thin curls have lots of surface area and light from a match or ferro rod. Use the ferro rod first and save the matches as backup. Build on a dry platform of split sticks, feed small pieces steadily, and dry the next fuel beside the fire.

interior_chunks.explanation: The dry inner wood was the right material in the wrong form. A chunk, no matter how dry, will not catch from a spark or match. Tinder must be fine - thin shavings, curls, or scrapings - so it heats up fast. Carve feather sticks or scrape fine shavings from the dry wood, then light them.

resinous_sources.scenario: You find an old pine stump. The wood near the base is heavy, amber colored, sticky, and smells strongly of pine - fatwood. A fallen birch lies nearby with loose bark curls. What do you use?

options.text: Scrape fatwood into fine dust and thin shavings for tinder
Peel the loose outer bark curls from the fallen birch for tinder

fatwood_tinder.explanation: Fatwood is pine heartwood soaked with resin. The resin repels water and burns hot and steady, so it works well in wet weather. Scraped dust catches a ferro rod spark, and thin shavings light from a match. Look for it in old stumps, roots, and where dead branches join the trunk. Never cut live trees to get it.

birch_bark.explanation: Birch bark contains natural oils and burns well even when damp. Take the thin papery outer layers from dead or fallen birch, or loose curls already shedding - stripping bark from living trees damages them and can kill them. Tear it thin or scrape it into fuzz for a ferro rod. Both birch bark and fatwood are excellent wet-weather tinders.

scenario: You're setting up camp in a dry pine forest with no posted fire restrictions. There is no existing fire ring. Wind is light. Before you light a fire, which step matters most for preventing an escaped fire?

options.text: Dig the fire pit at least 2 feet deep to hide the flames
Pick bare ground at least 15 feet from tents and brush, clear a 10-foot-wide circle to mineral soil, and have water and a shovel ready
Place the fire downwind of your tent so smoke blows away from camp
Ring the fire with rocks from the nearby creek

explanation: Most escaped campfires start when embers land in dry needles, grass, or duff around the fire. Current Forest Service (Smokey Bear) guidance is to keep the fire at least 15 feet from tents, vegetation, and low branches, clear a 10-foot-diameter area, and have water and a shovel ready before lighting. A very deep pit is unnecessary - about 1 foot is the guideline - and does not stop flying embers. Wind direction matters for comfort but does not prevent spread. Creek rocks can hold water and crack or burst when heated. In a dry pine forest, also consider whether you need a fire at all.

scenario: You're using a new ferro rod for the first time. You scrape it with the included striker over a pile of small twigs and leaves. You get only a few weak sparks, and nothing catches. What's the best fix?

options.text: Strike faster and lighter so the sparks fly farther
Scrape off the rod's black coating, press harder with slow strokes, and use fine fluffy tinder like petroleum-jelly cotton or fatwood dust
Switch to striking with the sharp cutting edge of your knife
Soak the twigs in hand sanitizer before striking

explanation: New ferro rods usually have a protective coating that must be scraped off before they spark well. Firm, slow strokes shed more hot metal than fast light flicks. Most importantly, twigs and leaves do not catch sparks - you need fine, fluffy tinder such as fluffed petroleum-jelly cotton, fatwood dust, birch bark fuzz, or plant down. The knife's cutting edge dulls the blade and is unsafe; use the striker or a square knife spine. Adding liquid fuels or sanitizer is risky and unnecessary.

scenario: It is 10 degrees F (-12 degrees C). Your disposable butane lighter has been in your outer jacket pocket all day. When you try to light your fire, it sparks but gives no flame, even though you can see fuel inside. What should you do?

options.text: Throw it away - it is broken
Warm the lighter in your hand or an inside pocket for a few minutes, then try again, and use your ferro rod or stormproof matches meanwhile
Hold the lighter near the tinder and click it faster
Heat the lighter over another flame to build pressure

explanation: Butane does not turn to gas well below about freezing, so a cold lighter may spark but make no flame. Warming it close to your body usually fixes the problem. Carry it in an inside pocket in cold weather. A ferro rod and stormproof matches are not affected by cold the same way, which is why you carry more than one ignition source. Never heat a lighter over a flame - it can burst.

scenario: You are done with your campfire for the night. You have a shovel and plenty of water. A friend says to just cover the coals with dirt so they go out. What is the right way to put it out?

options.text: Cover it with a thick layer of dirt and go to bed
Let it burn out on its own - it is small
Drown it with water until the hissing stops, stir the ashes and embers, drown it again, then feel with the back of your hand for heat
Pour one bucket of water over it and leave once the flames are gone

explanation: The Forest Service method is Drown, Stir, Drown, Feel. Dirt alone does not reliably put out embers - it can insulate coals so they stay hot and reignite hours later. One bucket often leaves hidden embers under logs and ash, which is why you stir and drown again. Never leave a fire to burn out on its own. Finish by feeling just above the ashes with the back of your hand: if it is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave.

scenario: A winter storm knocks out power for three days. Your house is getting cold. You have a portable generator, a charcoal grill, a camp stove, and a wood stove that was inspected this fall. Which is the safest way to stay warm?

options.text: Run the generator in the attached garage with the big door open and power a space heater
Bring the charcoal grill inside after the coals stop flaming
Burn seasoned wood in the inspected wood stove, keep combustibles 3 feet away, and make sure battery-powered CO and smoke alarms are working
Run the camp stove in the kitchen with a window cracked

explanation: A properly vented, inspected wood stove is designed for indoor heat. Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet away and have working battery-powered CO and smoke alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas. CDC says never to use generators, grills, or camp stoves inside a home, basement, or garage, even with doors or windows open - carbon monoxide builds up fast and has no smell. Generators belong outdoors at least 20 feet from doors, windows, and vents. Charcoal gives off CO even after the flames are gone.

scenario: You are stranded in 2 feet (60 cm) of snow in a forest and need a fire to warm up and melt water. Where and how should you build it?

options.text: Right on the snow under a big spruce with heavy snow on its branches, for shelter from wind
Inside your small tent, so the heat stays in
On a platform of thick logs laid side by side on the snow, in a spot sheltered from wind but with no snow-loaded branches overhead
In a deep hole dug in the snow so the fire is out of the wind

explanation: A fire built on snow melts down and drowns itself, so in deep snow you build a platform of thick logs to keep it up. Shelter from wind helps, but snow-loaded branches overhead will melt and dump snow on the fire - or on you. A fire in a snow hole sinks into meltwater. Never build a fire or run a stove inside a tent or closed shelter: carbon monoxide builds up fast, and the tent can catch fire. In shallow snow, dig down to bare ground instead.

scenario: You bought a cord of firewood in October to heat your home this winter. The seller says it was cut last month. You split a piece and the fresh face feels cool and damp. What should you do?

options.text: Burn it - all firewood is the same once it is in a hot stove
Burn it on low air settings so it lasts longer
Split it all, stack it off the ground with the top covered and sides open, and buy or use already-seasoned wood (20% moisture or less) for this winter
Store it in a closed shed so it stays out of the rain

explanation: Freshly cut wood can be 50% water or more. Burning it wastes heat, makes heavy smoke, and builds creosote in the chimney, which can lead to a chimney fire - especially on low, smoldering burns. EPA Burn Wise guidance is to burn wood at 20% moisture or less and season hardwood at least 12 months and softwood at least 6 months. Split wood dries faster, and it needs air flow: stack it off the ground with only the top covered. A closed shed with no air movement slows drying.
